USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should hold its current tariff posture and avoid further escalation while signaling willingness to negotiate. The midterm elections have just passed, removing the domestic political pressure that drove tariff escalation. With $250 billion in tariffs already in place covering roughly half of US-China trade, and China having retaliated on nearly all $130 billion of US exports it imports, the tariff war is near saturation. Further escalation to cover the remaining $267 billion in Chinese imports would impose significant costs on US consumers and firms with diminishing strategic leverage. The US should use the post-election window to open serious high-level negotiations.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.3 reflects a moderate but not existential threat to US interests. The trade war has already imposed real costs: soybean prices are down 20% (Brookings), farmers in the Midwest are feeling pain, and US companies operating in China face collateral damage. The $250 billion in tariffs already enacted represent roughly half of all US-China trade (Fox Business/Motley Fool), meaning the US has already deployed its major leverage. However, the US economy is large enough that Brookings characterizes this as 'a minor blip' overall, and the US has structural advantages — China cannot fully match US tariffs since it only imports $130 billion of US goods versus $506 billion the US imports from China. The threat is real but manageable.

The action score of -0.1 (hold) reflects the post-midterm strategic calculus. The Brookings analysis explicitly notes that 'the Trump administration sees this as a winning strategy for the midterm elections' and that 'after the 2018 elections, we're likely to see the two sides come together and negotiate something so that they can both save face.' The midterms have just occurred (November 6, 2018), removing the domestic political incentive for continued escalation. The Washington Post reports that trade talks have been complicated by crossed signals — China believed it had deals with Ross and Mnuchin that Trump vetoed — suggesting the US should now clarify its negotiating position rather than add more tariffs. China has signaled willingness to buy more US products and open markets. Holding current tariffs while pursuing negotiations is the optimal path: it preserves leverage, avoids further consumer/farmer pain, and exploits the post-election political window for a deal.
key_factors: $250B in US tariffs already in place covering ~half of US-China trade; further escalation has diminishing returns
Soybean prices down 20%; Midwest farmers and US auto exporters already hurting from Chinese retaliation
Post-midterm election window removes domestic political pressure for escalation
China has signaled willingness to buy more US products and open markets
US-China trade talks have been complicated by crossed signals; clarity needed
US has asymmetric leverage: China imports only $130B vs US imports of $506B from China

sources_cited.excerpt: The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent. This is not a big hit for the overall U.S. economy but it will hurt some specific sectors. After the 2018 elections, we're likely to see the two sides come together and negotiate something so that they can both save face.

sources_cited.excerpt: The $250 billion aggregate tariff amount... is about half of U.S.-China trade. President Trump has also indicated that if things don't go as to what he wants to happen, he's going to do it on the rest of it. Almost all the cards have been played here.

sources_cited.source_id: www.washingtonpost.com — How the U.S. and China misread the signals in the trade war
sources_cited.excerpt: Chinese leaders believed they had a trade agreement last year with Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, only to see President Trump veto it. In May, they reached a second deal with Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, but Trump again turned thumbs down.

sources_cited.source_id: www.cbsnews.com — Trade war with China: What you need to know
sources_cited.excerpt: China has promised to respond in kind, but it would be unable to match that amount since it imported only $130 billion of U.S. goods last year. Soybean prices fell to their lowest level in two years.
